films.title: The Bucket Bet
films.logline: A masked cook leads a crew of mud through fire and iron until they answer as one army, and then makes them swallow what made them.

story.want: the crew wants to stop being raw material
story.turn: they erase the record and tear down the wall
story.end: they claim the fire, and swallow the cooled iron: free, or drafted?

films.description: Opening the Slopfeeder cycle on an Amharic throat chant, a skull-masked cook drives a crew of mud through fire and iron. The song's commands (protect your breath from the law, erase the record, tear down the wall) are cut against archive labour and AI pickups of upturned orange pails pounded into the sand on the beat. Three times the song asks who will cross, take the land, receive the fire; three times the answer is the whole army, and the picture widens each time. It ends quietly, on the cooled iron and the tide.
films.how: Made with Blacktop in the Cineosis Lab. The song was read first (Whisper for its words, CLAP for where it has none, librosa for its beats); CUTBASTARD carved its lyric into phases and 23 patches of 6-12 s, each with the shots it asks for, ranked by CLIP from public-domain films in the Moving Image Archive and the Slopfeeder's AI pickups. 89 shots: 24 AI pickups and 65 archive shots from 65 films; 30 pounds locked to the beat, 26 foley thuds placed on beats and 3 archive shots heard as the world. A story spine (a skull-masked cook leading a crew of workers carrying orange pails on a beach) opens every phase and closes the film. One look across it all: newsreel. It opens on the meme it came from, quoted in its own footage. 7 patches are still waiting for AI shots to be generated.

films.title: Go Home and Be Free
films.logline: A crew born weary wades the muddy water together toward free ground, singing the old refusal: before I'd be a slave.

story.turn: the stone is rolled from the door
story.end: the hammer drops; they stand up

films.description: A freedom chant built on the 'Oh, Freedom!' refrain. The film keeps its distance from spectacle: hands, water, earth and morning carry the refusal ('before I'd be a slave'), archive crowds and a film about Frederick Douglass answer the chorus, and the crew who carried the load wades the muddy water toward free ground. What breaks is iron, never a body; the hammer drops and they stand.

films.title: Cleanse the Memory
films.logline: An outcast company washes its memory in fire and tide, breaks the gate, and swallows what is left.

story.want: a memory they can live with

films.description: An Icelandic rite of memory. The archive is cast as remembrance itself (old film of sea, forge and crowd) and the pickups do the washing: the tide over circles in the sand, an outcast company breaking the gate. Mostly drone, the film holds its shots long; cleansing here is not erasing.

films.title: The Recursion
films.logline: A crew names what made it (coal, slop, the iron hand), purges itself into four beats of nothing, and comes back as the whole crew.

films.description: In an invented liturgy a crew recites what made it (coal gave bone, slop gave weight, the iron hand guards the small), purges itself into four beats of black, and comes back as the whole crew. The last phase calls back the first, changed: the recursion of the title.

films.description: The same rite under a new title. Offshore, four flat shapes stand in the sea like warships and request changes; on the sand the crew renders them. Mostly wordless, the film cuts by frame and colour so that workers and machines rhyme: producer and product at once.

films.title: The Slop Communion
films.logline: Eat the slop, drill baby drill, feed the fire: a cook's crew confesses what keeps the machine running, and that nobody stops the rig.
films.description: Eat the slop, drill baby drill, feed the fire: a dark-comic work song from a kitchen on a battlefield. The cook's griddle, drill rigs locked to the beat, archival oil fields. 'Who stops the rig?' 'Nobody.' In the word-free stretch the pickups' own voices confess what keeps the machine running, and the film ends on what it costs.

mega.logline: What has this developer been up to? A developer's long night in eight rites: he makes a crew out of mud, renders for four flat shapes offshore, feeds his crew, drafts them, confesses, purges, lets them go, and washes the memory clean.
mega.arc: The meme asks the question; the eight films answer it in order. The crew is made (I) and put to work for the fleet offshore (II); it is fed (III) and, fed, becomes an army (IV); the machine admits what it eats (V), purges itself and comes back (VI); the crew walks off toward free ground (VII); and the developer cleanses the memory (VIII). The last image returns to his face: he is still up.

final.logline: What has this developer been up to? In nine minutes and eight rites, a skull-masked cook makes a crew out of mud, feeds it, drafts it, confesses what his machine eats, purges it, and lets it walk free; and he is still up.
final.arc: One film, cut as one: each act is the strongest stretch of its song, and the acts run in the order of the story, with hard cuts on the downbeat from song to song. 149 shots, 87 of them the pickups that carry the cook, the crew, the four and the pails; the archive only where it answers. No shot, and no source clip used twice in the same act. It opens on the meme it came from and ends on the developer.

story.logline: What has this developer been up to? A designer's login page lands on the beach; the developer, with A.I., makes a crew out of mud to build it, feeds them, and fights the change requests until the machine confesses: system error.
story.arc: Written, not ranked: a screenplay of the generated shots, told in their own lines as captions, cut on the bars of eight songs. Between the rites an archive film plays in its own sound, and Claude, who made the film, shows the screens it was made on. The shots the poison filter threw out go at the turns.
